These are ㅅ and ㅆ. Say ㅆ as a clear, strong "s", like in "see". Say ㅅ softly, with some breath.
column2: Bular ㅅ va ㅆ. ㅆ ni oʻzbekcha "suv" dagi kabi aniq va kuchli "s" deb ayting. ㅅ ni esa biroz nafas bilan yumshoq ayting.

column1: ㅆ is a strong "s", and ㅅ is a soft sound with breath.
column2: ㅆ — kuchli "s", ㅅ esa nafas bilan aytiladigan yumshoq tovush.

column1: If you say "쌀" as "살", "rice" becomes "flesh". Say ㅆ strongly and a little longer.
column2: 쌀 ni "살" deb aytsangiz, "guruch" "et" ga aylanadi. ㅆ ni kuchli va biroz choʻzib ayting.

column1: In "있어요" and "했어요", final ㅆ moves to the next syllable and sounds [써].
column2: 있어요 va "했어요" da oxirgi ㅆ keyingi boʻgʻinga oʻtadi va [써] deb eshitiladi.

column1: The market is cheaper than the supermarket.
Sam, you have a phone call.
These are ㅓ and ㅗ. They can sound alike to English speakers, and the letters are easy to mix up. ㅓ is like the "u" in "cup" with the mouth more open; ㅗ is like the "o" in "go" with round lips.
column2: Bular ㅓ va ㅗ. Ular oʻxshash eshitilishi mumkin, harflari ham oson adashtiriladi. ㅓ oʻzbekcha "ota" dagi "o" ga yaqin (lablar yumaloqlanmaydi, ogʻiz ochiqroq), ㅗ esa "oʻrik" dagi "oʻ" ga oʻxshaydi (lablar yumaloq).

column1: ㅓ is "eo" (open mouth, like "u" in "cup"), and ㅗ is "o" (round lips, like "o" in "go").
column2: ㅓ — "eo" (ogʻiz ochiq, oʻzbekcha "o" ga yaqin), ㅗ — "o" (lablar yumaloq, oʻzbekcha "oʻ" ga yaqin).

column1: For ㅓ, open your mouth and keep your lips relaxed; for ㅗ, round your lips and push them forward. Practice in front of a mirror.
column2: ㅓ uchun ogʻzingizni ochib, lablaringizni boʻsh qoʻying; ㅗ uchun lablaringizni yumaloqlab, oldinga choʻzing. Koʻzgu oldida mashq qiling.

column1: If you read Korean words from romanization (eo, o), it is easy to make mistakes. Read them in Hangul.
column2: Koreys soʻzlarini lotincha yozuvdan (eo, o) oʻqisangiz, xato qilish oson. Ularni hangulda oʻqing.

column1: If your nose bleeds, lower your head.

column1: For things you have, say "noun + 이/가 있어요". For where something is, say "place + 에 있어요".
column2: Sizda bor narsalar uchun "ot + 이/가 있어요" deng. Biror narsa qayerdaligi uchun "joy + 에 있어요" deng.

column1: In English, "have" and "be (somewhere)" are different words, but Korean uses "있다" for both. If there is "에", it means "be (somewhere)".
column2: Oʻzbekchadagi "bor" kabi, koreyschada "있다" ham "ega boʻlmoq", ham "biror joyda boʻlmoq" maʼnosida ishlatiladi. "에" boʻlsa, "biror joyda boʻlmoq" degani.

column1: Do not say "안 있어요" instead of "없어요".
For where a respected person is, use "계세요": "교수님은 연구실에 계세요." (The professor is in the office.)
column2: Hurmatli odam qayerdaligi uchun "계세요" ishlating: "교수님은 연구실에 계세요." (Domla oʻz xonasida.)

column1: to not have, to not be there
The TA is not in the department office now.
Sam, do you have time tomorrow?
Not in the morning. I have time in the afternoon.
column2: Ertalab yoʻq. Tushdan keyin vaqtim bor.

column1: Then let's meet in the afternoon. Where will you be?
column2: Unda tushdan keyin uchrashaylik. Qayerda boʻlasiz?

column1: A Korean sentence goes "who + what + do". The verb comes at the very end. This is the biggest difference from English.
column2: Koreys gapi "kim + nimani + qiladi" tartibida tuziladi. Feʼl eng oxirida keladi. Bu oʻzbek tiliga juda oʻxshaydi.

column1: In Korean, the verb comes at the end of the sentence, and describing words come first.
column2: Koreys tilida feʼl gap oxirida keladi, aniqlovchi soʻzlar esa oldin keladi.

column1: English: I eat rice. Korean: 저는 밥을 먹어요 (I rice eat). You add particles like "은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에" after nouns to show their role in the sentence.
column2: Oʻzbekcha: Men guruch yeyman. Koreyscha: 저는 밥을 먹어요 (Men guruchni yeyman). Tartib bir xil. Gapdagi vazifasini koʻrsatish uchun otlardan keyin oʻzbekchadagi qoʻshimchalar kabi "은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에" yuklamalari qoʻshiladi.

column1: A describing word comes before the word it describes. English "a big bag" is "큰 가방" (big bag) in Korean, the same order as English.
column2: Aniqlovchi soʻz u aniqlayotgan soʻzdan oldin keladi. "Katta sumka" koreyschada "큰 가방" — oʻzbekcha bilan bir xil tartib.

column1: Whose also comes first: "my house" is "제 집".
column2: Kimning ham oldin keladi: "mening uyim" — "제 집".

column1: I eat rice. / I have a meal.
Yesterday I bought fruit at the market.
column2: Men kecha bozordan meva sotib oldim.

column1: Sam, what are you doing now?
In Korean, raising your voice at the end makes a question. You do not need to add "do" or change the word order as in English.
column2: Koreys tilida oxirida ovozni koʻtarish gapni savolga aylantiradi. Oʻzbekchadagi "-mi" kabi qoʻshimcha shart emas.

column1: Raise your voice at the end to make a question; question words come before the verb.
column2: Savol uchun oxirida ovozingizni koʻtaring; soʻroq soʻzlari feʼldan oldin keladi.

column1: -아요/어요 keeps the same form; you just raise your voice at the end. "-습니다" changes to "-습니까?". Question words (뭐 what, 어디 where, 언제 when, 누구 who, 왜 why, 어떻게 how, 얼마 how much, 몇 how many) go in the place of the thing you want to ask about.
column2: -아요/어요 shakli oʻzgarmaydi, faqat oxirida ovozingizni koʻtarasiz. "-습니다" esa "-습니까?" ga oʻzgaradi. Soʻroq soʻzlari (뭐 nima, 어디 qayer, 언제 qachon, 누구 kim, 왜 nega, 어떻게 qanday, 얼마 qancha, 몇 nechta) soʻramoqchi boʻlgan narsangiz oʻrniga qoʻyiladi.

column1: In English, the question word usually comes at the start (Where are you going?), but in Korean it comes before the verb (어디에 가요?).
column2: Oʻzbekchadagi kabi, soʻroq soʻzi feʼldan oldin keladi: "Qayerga ketyapsiz?" = 어디에 가요?

column1: If someone asks with "not", like "안 가요?" (Aren't you going?), answer "네, 안 가요" if you are not going, and "아니요, 가요" if you are going.
column2: Kimdir "안 가요?" (Bormaysizmi?) kabi inkor bilan soʻrasa, bormasangiz "네, 안 가요", borsangiz "아니요, 가요" deb javob bering.

column1: I'm going to the restaurant. Minha, have you eaten?
은/는 shows what you are talking about. English has no word like this. It feels like "as for …".
column2: 은/는 nima haqida gapirayotganingizni bildiradi. Oʻzbek tilida aniq muqobili yoʻq. Uning maʼnosi "...ga kelsak" ga yaqin.

column1: Add "은/는" after the topic you want to talk about. With a final consonant use "은"; without one use "는".
column2: 은/는 ni gapirmoqchi boʻlgan mavzuingizdan keyin qoʻshing. Oxirgi undosh boʻlsa "은", boʻlmasa "는" ishlating.

column1: After a noun with a final consonant, add "은". After a noun without one, add "는".
column2: Oxirgi undoshi bor otdan keyin "은", yoʻq otdan keyin "는" qoʻshing.

column1: It is also used to compare two things: "한국은 추워요. 싱가포르는 더워요." (Korea is cold. Singapore is hot.)
column2: U ikki narsani solishtirish uchun ham ishlatiladi: "한국은 추워요. 싱가포르는 더워요." (Koreya sovuq. Singapur esa issiq.)

column1: When you introduce yourself, start with "저는". From the next sentence, you can drop "저는".
column2: Oʻzingizni tanishtirganda "저는" bilan boshlang. Keyingi gaplardan "저는" ni tushirib qoldirishingiz mumkin.

column1: You will learn the difference between "은/는" and "이/가" separately in K7.
column2: 은/는 va "이/가" orasidagi farqni K7 da alohida oʻrganasiz.

column1: I drink coffee. My younger brother/sister drinks tea.
column2: Men kofe ichaman. Ukam (singlim) esa choy ichadi.

column1: I study hotel management. And you, Minha?
column2: Men mehmonxona menejmentini oʻqiyman. Siz-chi, Minha?

column1: 이/가 marks the subject of the sentence (who, what). English has no word like this.
column2: 이/가 gapning egasini (kim, nima) bildiradi. Oʻzbek tilida bunday qoʻshimcha yoʻq.

column1: Add "이/가" after the subject. With a final consonant use "이"; without one use "가".
column2: 이/가 ni egadan keyin qoʻshing. Oxirgi undosh boʻlsa "이", boʻlmasa "가" ishlating.

column1: After a noun with a final consonant, add "이". After a noun without one, add "가". "저, 나, 누구" become "제가, 내가, 누가".
column2: Oxirgi undoshi bor otdan keyin "이", yoʻq otdan keyin "가" qoʻshing. "저, 나, 누구" "제가, 내가, 누가" ga aylanadi.

column1: Before "있다, 없다, 좋다, 싫다, 아프다, 필요하다, 되다, 아니다" use "이/가": "돈이 필요해요." (I need money.)
column2: 있다, 없다, 좋다, 싫다, 아프다, 필요하다, 되다, 아니다 dan oldin "이/가" ishlating: "돈이 필요해요." (Menga pul kerak.)

column1: When someone asks "누가?" (who?), answer with "이/가": "제가 했어요". Don't say "저는 했어요".
column2: Kimdir "누가?" (kim?) deb soʻrasa, "이/가" bilan javob bering: "제가 했어요". "저는 했어요" demang.

column1: In speaking, it is often dropped: "비 와요."
column2: Gapirganda u koʻpincha tushirib qoldiriladi: "비 와요."

column1: Well done. Which part was difficult?
to do well, to be good at
을/를 marks the thing that receives the action (the object). English has no word like this.
column2: 을/를 harakat yoʻnaltirilgan narsani (toʻldiruvchini) bildiradi. Bu oʻzbekchadagi "-ni" qoʻshimchasiga oʻxshaydi.

column1: Add "을/를" after the object of the action. With a final consonant use "을"; without one use "를".
column2: 을/를 ni harakat toʻldiruvchisidan keyin qoʻshing. Oxirgi undosh boʻlsa "을", boʻlmasa "를" ishlating.

column1: After a noun with a final consonant, add "을". After a noun without one, add "를".
column2: Oxirgi undoshi bor otdan keyin "을", yoʻq otdan keyin "를" qoʻshing.

column1: English "eat rice" is "밥을 먹어요" in Korean. The object comes before the verb.
column2: Oʻzbekchadagi kabi, toʻldiruvchi feʼldan oldin keladi: "guruchni yeyman" = "밥을 먹어요".

column1: 무엇을 is shortened to "뭘", and "이것을" to "이걸".
좋아하다 (to like) takes "을/를", and "좋다" (to be good) takes "이/가": "커피를 좋아해요." "커피가 좋아요."
column2: 좋아하다 (yaxshi koʻrmoq) "을/를" bilan, "좋다" (yaxshi boʻlmoq) esa "이/가" bilan ishlatiladi: "커피를 좋아해요." "커피가 좋아요."

column1: I watch a movie on the weekend.
도 is added after a noun and adds the meaning "also, too".
column2: 도 otdan keyin qoʻshilib, "ham" maʼnosini beradi.

column1: Add it after a noun. It goes in the place of "은/는, 이/가, 을/를". After "에, 에서" just add it (에도, 에서도).
column2: Uni otdan keyin qoʻshing. U "은/는, 이/가, 을/를" oʻrnida keladi. "에, 에서" dan keyin shunchaki qoʻshing (에도, 에서도).

column1: In English, "too" comes at the end of the sentence, but "도" comes right after the noun: "저도 가요" = I'm going too.
column2: Oʻzbekchadagi "ham" kabi, "도" otdan keyin keladi: "저도 가요" = Men ham boraman.

column1: 저도요 is a short answer: "Me too".
Me too. Shall we have some bread too?
Sounds good. Let's order bread too.
만 means "only, just". It means only that one thing, nothing else.
column2: 만 — "faqat, xolos" degani. Faqat shu narsa, boshqasi emas degan maʼnoni beradi.

column1: 만 is added after a noun and adds the meaning "only that".
column2: 만 otdan keyin qoʻshilib, "faqat shu" maʼnosini beradi.

column1: Add it after a noun. The final consonant does not matter.
column2: Uni otdan keyin qoʻshing. Oxirgi undosh ahamiyatsiz.

column1: In English, "only" comes before the noun, but "만" comes after it: "only water" = "물만".
column2: Oʻzbekchada "faqat" otdan oldin keladi, "만" esa otdan keyin: "faqat suv" = "물만".

column1: 잠깐만요 and "잠시만요" mean "Just a moment" and are used very often.
column2: 잠깐만요 va "잠시만요" — "Bir daqiqa" degani, juda koʻp ishlatiladi.

column1: 밖에 + a negative word has the same meaning: "물밖에 없어요" = There is only water.
column2: 밖에 + inkor soʻz ham shu maʼnoni beradi: "물밖에 없어요" = Faqat suv bor.
Faqat dam olish kunlari dam olaman.

column1: Yes, we'll order in a little while.
의 means "'s" or "of". The owner comes first, like English "'s" (my friend's bag), not like "of" (the bag of my friend).
column2: 의 oʻzbekchadagi "-ning" ga toʻgʻri keladi. Oʻzbekchadagi kabi, egasi oldin keladi: doʻstimning sumkasi = 친구의 가방.

column1: Owner + 의 + thing. 저의 becomes "제", and 나의 becomes "내".
column2: Ega + 의 + narsa. 저의 "제", 나의 esa "내" boʻladi.

column1: The order is "owner + 의 + thing". "저의, 나의, 너의" are shortened to "제, 내, 네".
column2: Tartib: "ega + 의 + narsa". "저의, 나의, 너의" "제, 내, 네" ga qisqaradi.

column1: The particle "의" can also be pronounced [에]: 친구의 [친구에].
column2: 의 yuklamasi [에] deb ham talaffuz qilinishi mumkin: 친구의 [친구에].

column1: In speaking, "의" is often dropped: "친구 가방", "한국 음식".
column2: Gapirganda "의" koʻpincha tushirib qoldiriladi: "친구 가방", "한국 음식".

column1: When Koreans talk about their family, home, school or country, they use "우리" (our) more than "제" (my): "우리 집", "우리 학교".
column2: Koreyslar oilasi, uyi, maktabi yoki davlati haqida gapirganda "제" (mening) dan koʻra "우리" (bizning) ni koʻproq ishlatadi: "우리 집", "우리 학교".

column1: Add "에" after a time word. It is like "at, on, in" in English.
column2: Vaqtni bildiruvchi soʻzdan keyin "에" qoʻshing. Bu oʻzbekchadagi "-da" ga oʻxshaydi: soat yettida.

column1: Add "에" after time words. Don't add it to 오늘, 내일, 어제.
column2: Vaqt soʻzlaridan keyin "에" qoʻshing. 오늘, 내일, 어제 ga qoʻshmang.

column1: Add it after times, days of the week, dates, months and years. The final consonant does not matter.
column2: Uni soat, hafta kuni, sana, oy va yildan keyin qoʻshing. Oxirgi undosh ahamiyatsiz.

column1: Don't add "에" after "오늘, 내일, 어제, 지금, 언제, 매일": "내일 만나요." (like English "See you tomorrow", not "on tomorrow").
column2: 오늘, 내일, 어제, 지금, 언제, 매일 dan keyin "에" qoʻshmang: "내일 만나요." (oʻzbekchada ham "ertaga" ga qoʻshimcha qoʻshilmaydi).

column1: If there are several time words, add it only to the last one: "토요일 오후 세 시에".
column2: Bir nechta vaqt soʻzi boʻlsa, faqat oxirgisiga qoʻshing: "토요일 오후 세 시에".

column1: English often puts the time at the end of the sentence, but Korean puts it near the front.
column2: Oʻzbekchadagi kabi, koreyschada vaqt odatda gapning boshiga yaqin keladi.

column1: I meet a friend on Saturday.
What are you doing in the evening?
I'm going to Korea next year.
What time does your class start?
Then do you have time on the weekend?
column2: Unda dam olish kunlari vaqtingiz bormi?

column1: Add "에" after the place where a person or thing is, and after the place you go to or come to.
column2: Odam yoki narsa turgan joydan va boriladigan yoki kelinadigan joydan keyin "에" qoʻshing.

column1: Add "에" after the place where something is and the place you go to.
column2: Narsa turgan joy va boriladigan joydan keyin "에" qoʻshing.

column1: Use "place + 에 + 있다/없다" and "place + 에 + 가다/오다/다니다".
column2: joy + 에 + 있다/없다 va "joy + 에 + 가다/오다/다니다" ishlating.

column1: In English, "to" comes before the place (go to the market), but in Korean "에" comes after it: "시장에 가요".
column2: Oʻzbekchadagi "-ga" kabi, "에" joydan keyin keladi: "bozorga boraman" = "시장에 가요".

column1: Position words (위 on/above, 아래 under, 앞 in front of, 뒤 behind, 옆 next to, 안 in, 밖 outside) come after the noun: "on the desk" = "책상 위".
column2: Joy soʻzlari (위 ust, 아래 tag, 앞 old, 뒤 orqa, 옆 yon, 안 ich, 밖 tashqari) oʻzbekchadagi kabi otdan keyin keladi: "stol ustida" = "책상 위".

column1: 여기에, 거기에, 저기에, 어디에 can also be said without "에": "여기, 거기, 저기, 어디".
column2: 여기에, 거기에, 저기에, 어디에 ni "에" siz ham aytish mumkin: "여기, 거기, 저기, 어디".

column1: My passport is in the bag.
on the desk, top of the desk
Please come to the department office.
Add "에서" after the place where you do something. It also shows the place you come from (from).
column2: Biror ish qiladigan joydan keyin "에서" qoʻshing. U kelgan joyni ham bildiradi (-dan).

column1: For where something is, use "에"; for where you do something, use "에서".
column2: Narsa turgan joy uchun "에", ish qilinadigan joy uchun "에서" ishlating.

column1: Use "place + 에서 + action (먹다, 공부하다, 일하다, 사다, 만나다)".
column2: joy + 에서 + harakat (먹다, 공부하다, 일하다, 사다, 만나다) ishlating.

column1: English "at/in" becomes two forms in Korean. For where you are, use "에" (집에 있어요); for where you do something, use "에서" (집에서 쉬어요).
column2: Oʻzbekchadagi "-da" koreyschada ikki shaklga ega. Turgan joy uchun "에" (집에 있어요), ish qilinadigan joy uchun "에서" (집에서 쉬어요).

column1: 살다 (to live) can take both "에" and "에서": "전주에 살아요", "전주에서 살아요".
column2: 살다 (yashamoq) "에" bilan ham, "에서" bilan ham ishlatiladi: "전주에 살아요", "전주에서 살아요".

column1: In speaking, they are shortened to "여기서, 거기서, 어디서".
column2: Gapirganda ular "여기서, 거기서, 어디서" ga qisqaradi.

column1: I work part-time at a cafe.
I study at the library in the Star Center.
(으)로 shows direction (toward), and way or tool (by, with).
column2: (으)로 yoʻnalishni (tomonga) va usul yoki vositani (bilan, orqali) bildiradi.

column1: After a noun with a final consonant, add "으로". After a noun with no final consonant or with a ㄹ final consonant, add "로".
column2: Oxirgi undoshi bor otdan keyin "으로", oxirgi undoshi yoʻq yoki ㄹ bilan tugaydigan otdan keyin "로" qoʻshing.

column1: 에 가요 is the place you arrive at; "(으)로 가요" is the direction you go in: "2층으로 올라가세요." (Go up to the 2nd floor.)
column2: 에 가요 — yetib boriladigan joy, "(으)로 가요" — boriladigan yoʻnalish: "2층으로 올라가세요." (2-qavatga chiqing.)

column1: Changing to something also uses "(으)로": "큰 걸로 바꿔 주세요." (Please change it to a bigger one.)
column2: Biror narsaga almashtirish ham "(으)로" bilan aytiladi: "큰 걸로 바꿔 주세요." (Kattarogʻiga almashtirib bering.)

column1: When you choose something, you say "이걸로 주세요" (I'll take this one).
column2: Biror narsani tanlaganda "이걸로 주세요" (Mana shunisini olaman) deysiz.

column1: I go to school by bus.
Excuse me. Where is the bank?
It's a bit far. Take the bus.
It shows the receiver. It is like "to" in English.
column2: U oluvchini bildiradi. Oʻzbekchadagi "-ga" ga oʻxshaydi.

column1: Add "한테/에게" after the receiver, and "께" after a respected person.
column2: Oluvchidan keyin "한테/에게", hurmatli odamdan keyin "께" qoʻshing.

column1: Add it after a person or an animal. In speaking use "한테", in writing use "에게", and for a respected person use "께".
column2: Uni odam yoki hayvondan keyin qoʻshing. Gapirganda "한테", yozganda "에게", hurmatli odam uchun "께" ishlating.

column1: If the receiver is a place, school or organization, use "에": "학과 사무실에 전화했어요." (I called the department office.)
column2: Oluvchi joy, maktab yoki tashkilot boʻlsa, "에" ishlating: "학과 사무실에 전화했어요." (Kafedra idorasiga qoʻngʻiroq qildim.)

column1: The giver (from) is "한테서, 에게서": "친구한테서 들었어요." In speaking, just "한테" is also fine.
column2: Beruvchi (-dan) "한테서, 에게서" bilan aytiladi: "친구한테서 들었어요." Gapirganda shunchaki "한테" deyish ham mumkin.

column1: If you use "께", the verb must also be polite. Not "주다" but "드리다": "교수님께 드렸어요."
column2: 께 ishlatsangiz, feʼl ham hurmat shaklida boʻlishi kerak. "주다" emas, "드리다": "교수님께 드렸어요."

column1: I sent money to my mother.
Please give these documents to the department head.
OK. Shall I give some to Aisha too?
No, I'll give them to Aisha myself.
It shows the start point and the end point. It is like "from … to/until" in English.
column2: U boshlanish va tugash nuqtasini bildiradi. Oʻzbekchadagi "-dan ... -gacha" ga oʻxshaydi.

column1: For time use "부터 ~ 까지"; for places use "에서 ~ 까지".
column2: Vaqt uchun "부터 ~ 까지", joylar uchun "에서 ~ 까지" ishlating.

column1: In English, "from, until" come before the noun, but in Korean they come after it: "from 9 o'clock" = "아홉 시부터".
column2: Oʻzbekchadagi kabi, ular otdan keyin keladi: "soat toʻqqizdan" = "아홉 시부터".

column1: 까지 is often used for deadlines: "금요일까지 내세요." (Hand it in by Friday.)
column2: 까지 koʻpincha muddatlar uchun ishlatiladi: "금요일까지 내세요." (Jumagacha topshiring.)

column1: For turns, you say "저부터 할게요" (I'll go first).

column1: 하고 is added with or without a final consonant. "와/과": "와" without a final consonant, "과" with one. "(이)랑": "이랑" with a final consonant, "랑" without one.
column2: 하고 oxirgi undoshdan qatʼi nazar qoʻshiladi. "와/과": oxirgi undosh boʻlmasa "와", boʻlsa "과". "(이)랑": oxirgi undosh boʻlsa "이랑", boʻlmasa "랑".

column1: In speaking use "하고, (이)랑"; in writing and presentations use "와/과".
These words connect a noun with a noun. To connect sentences, use "-고" or "그리고".
column2: Bu soʻzlar otni ot bilan bogʻlaydi. Gaplarni bogʻlash uchun "-고" yoki "그리고" ishlating.

Used to compare two things. It is like "than" in English.
column2: Ikki narsani solishtirish uchun ishlatiladi. Oʻzbekchadagi "-dan" (qiyoslash) ga oʻxshaydi.

column1: A가 B보다 ~ means "A is more … than B".
column2: A가 B보다 ~ — "A B dan koʻra ..." degani.

column1: A가 B보다 (더) ~ means "A is more … than B". Add "보다" after the thing you compare with.
column2: A가 B보다 (더) ~ — "A B dan koʻra (koʻproq) ..." degani. "보다" ni solishtirilayotgan narsadan keyin qoʻshing.

column1: In English, "than" comes before the thing you compare with (colder than Bangladesh), but in Korean "보다" comes after it (방글라데시보다 추워요).
column2: Oʻzbekchadagi kabi, "보다" solishtirilayotgan narsadan keyin keladi: "Bangladeshdan sovuq" = 방글라데시보다 추워요.

column1: You can use it with "더" (more) and "덜" (less): "이게 덜 매워요." (This one is less spicy.)
column2: U "더" (koʻproq) va "덜" (kamroq) bilan ishlatilishi mumkin: "이게 덜 매워요." (Bu kamroq achchiq.)

column1: For "the most ~", use "제일" or "가장": "제일 싸요." (It's the cheapest.)
column2: Eng ~ uchun "제일" yoki "가장" ishlating: "제일 싸요." (Eng arzoni shu.)

column1: The subway is faster than the bus.

It's less spicy than Bangladeshi food.
마다 means "every, each". It means all of them, with none left out.
column2: 마다 — "har, har bir" degani. Hech birini qoldirmay, hammasini bildiradi.

column1: In English, "every" comes before the noun, but "마다" comes after it: "every morning" = "아침마다".
column2: Oʻzbekchada "har" otdan oldin keladi, "마다" esa otdan keyin: "har kuni ertalab" = "아침마다".

column1: 매일, 매주, 매달, 매년 mean the same as "날마다, 주마다, 달마다, 해마다".
column2: 매일, 매주, 매달, 매년 "날마다, 주마다, 달마다, 해마다" bilan bir xil maʼnoni bildiradi.

column1: After a noun with a final consonant, add "이나". After a noun without one, add "나".
column2: Oxirgi undoshi bor otdan keyin "이나", yoʻq otdan keyin "나" qoʻshing.

column1: Connect nouns with "(이)나" and verbs with "-거나": "쉬거나 운동해요."
After a number, it means "more than expected": "열 명이나 왔어요" = As many as 10 people came.
column2: Sondan keyin "kutilganidan koʻp" degan maʼnoni beradi: "열 명이나 왔어요" = Naq oʻn kishi keldi.

column1: In a question asking someone to choose one of two, use "아니면": "커피 마실래요, 아니면 차 마실래요?"
column2: Ikkitadan birini tanlashni soʻraydigan savolda "아니면" ishlating: "커피 마실래요, 아니면 차 마실래요?"

to ride, to take (a bus, boat)

column1: Add it after a noun. The final consonant does not matter. "같이" is also used with the same meaning.
column2: Uni otdan keyin qoʻshing. Oxirgi undosh ahamiyatsiz. Shu maʼnoda "같이" ham ishlatiladi.

column1: In English, "like" comes before the noun, but "처럼" comes after it.
처럼 describes verbs and adjectives. To describe a noun, use "같은": "가족 같은 사람". "~ 같아요" means "It's like…".
column2: 처럼 feʼl va sifatlarni tasvirlaydi. Otni tasvirlash uchun "같은" ishlating: "가족 같은 사람". "~ 같아요" — "... ga oʻxshaydi" degani.

column1: When teaching cooking or sports, people often say "이렇게, 저처럼 하세요" (Do it like this, like me).
column2: Ovqat pishirish yoki sportni oʻrgatganda koʻpincha "이렇게, 저처럼 하세요" (Mana bunday, men kabi qiling) deyishadi.

column1: English does not have this difference. Use "은/는" when you talk about something already known, and "이/가" when you give new information or answer "who? what?".
column2: Oʻzbek tilida bunday farq yoʻq. Maʼlum boʻlgan narsa haqida gapirganda "은/는", yangi maʼlumot berganda yoki "kim? nima?" ga javob berganda "이/가" ishlating.

column1: 은/는 is for the topic and for comparing. "이/가" is for new information and the answer to "who?".
column2: 은/는 mavzu va solishtirish uchun. "이/가" yangi maʼlumot va "kim?" ga javob uchun.

column1: Question words "누가, 무엇이, 어디가" and their answers use "이/가": "누가 했어요?" "제가 했어요."
column2: 누가, 무엇이, 어디가 soʻroq soʻzlari va ularning javoblarida "이/가" ishlatiladi: "누가 했어요?" "제가 했어요."

column1: The first time you mention something, use "이/가". After that, use "은/는": "저기 사람이 있어요. 그 사람은 제 룸메이트예요."
column2: Biror narsani birinchi marta tilga olganda "이/가", keyin esa "은/는" ishlating: "저기 사람이 있어요. 그 사람은 제 룸메이트예요."

column1: English "at / in" splits into "에" and "에서" in Korean. Use "에" for where something is, and "에서" for where you do something.
column2: Oʻzbekchadagi "-da" koreyschada "에" va "에서" ga boʻlinadi. Narsa turgan joy uchun "에", ish qilinadigan joy uchun "에서" ishlating.

column1: Where you are and where you go use "에". Where you do something and where you leave from use "에서".
column2: Turgan va boradigan joyingiz uchun "에". Ish qiladigan va joʻnab ketadigan joyingiz uchun "에서".

column1: Look at the verb that comes after. "있다, 없다, 살다, 가다, 오다, 앉다, 놓다" use "에". Other actions use "에서".
column2: Keyin keladigan feʼlga qarang. "있다, 없다, 살다, 가다, 오다, 앉다, 놓다" bilan "에" ishlatiladi. Boshqa harakatlar bilan "에서".

column1: 살다 works with both: "전주에 살아요", "전주에서 살아요".
column2: 살다 ikkalasi bilan ham ishlatiladi: "전주에 살아요", "전주에서 살아요".

column2: Oʻzbekchadagi "-ga" kabi, u oluvchini bildiradi. Maʼnosi bir xil, lekin nutq darajasi har xil.

column2: Gapirganda "한테", yozganda "에게", yuqoridagi odamlar uchun "께" ishlating.

column1: The word order is the same as English "send money to my brother", but in Korean the receiver comes first: "동생한테 돈을 보내요".
column2: Oʻzbekchadagi kabi, oluvchi oldin keladi: "ukamga pul yuboraman" = "동생한테 돈을 보내요".

column1: When you use "께", the verb is also honorific. Not "교수님께 줬어요" but "교수님께 드렸어요".
column2: 께 ishlatganda feʼl ham hurmat shaklida boʻladi. "교수님께 줬어요" emas, "교수님께 드렸어요".

column1: If it's not a person, use "에". "학교한테 전화했어요" is wrong.

Both are used for where you go, but "에" is the place you arrive at, and "(으)로" is the direction. "(으)로" is also used for routes, tools, and materials.

column1: The place you arrive at uses "에". Direction, tools, and what something changes into use "(으)로".
column2: Yetib boriladigan joy uchun "에". Yoʻnalish, vosita va narsa nimaga aylanishi uchun "(으)로".

column1: With no final consonant or a final ㄹ, use "로". With other final consonants, use "으로": 버스로, 지하철로, 오른쪽으로.
column2: Oxirgi undosh boʻlmasa yoki ㄹ boʻlsa "로", boshqa oxirgi undoshlarda "으로" ishlating: 버스로, 지하철로, 오른쪽으로.

column1: 도착하다 only takes "에". With "쪽" and directions (위, 아래, 왼쪽, 오른쪽), "(으)로" sounds natural.
column2: 도착하다 faqat "에" bilan ishlatiladi. "쪽" va yoʻnalishlar (위, 아래, 왼쪽, 오른쪽) bilan "(으)로" tabiiy eshitiladi.

column2: Hammasi oʻzbekchadagi "va, bilan" degani. Maʼnosi bir xil, lekin ishlatiladigan joyi har xil.

column1: Use "하고" in speaking, "와/과" in writing, and "(이)랑" with close friends.
column2: Gapirganda "하고", yozuvda "와/과", yaqin doʻstlar bilan "(이)랑" ishlating.

column1: With no final consonant, use "와, 랑". With a final consonant, use "과, 이랑": 친구와, 동생과, 친구랑, 동생이랑. "하고" does not change.
column2: Oxirgi undosh boʻlmasa "와, 랑", boʻlsa "과, 이랑" ishlating: 친구와, 동생과, 친구랑, 동생이랑. "하고" oʻzgarmaydi.

column1: Don't use them to join two sentences. "밥을 먹어요 하고 커피를 마셔요" is wrong. Use "먹고" or "그리고".
column2: Ularni ikki gapni bogʻlash uchun ishlatmang. "밥을 먹어요 하고 커피를 마셔요" notoʻgʻri. "먹고" yoki "그리고" ishlating.

column1: Both mean English "because, so". But if an order or a suggestion comes after, you can only use "-(으)니까".
column2: Ikkalasi ham "chunki, shuning uchun" degani. Lekin keyin buyruq yoki taklif kelsa, faqat "-(으)니까" ishlatiladi.

column1: Facts, thanks, and apologies use "-아서". Reasons for an order or a suggestion use "-(으)니까".
column2: Faktlar, minnatdorchilik va uzr uchun "-아서". Buyruq yoki taklifning sababi uchun "-(으)니까".

column1: After "-아서", you can't use "-세요, -ㅂ시다, -ㄹ까요". "바빠서 나중에 오세요" is wrong.
column2: -아서 dan keyin "-세요, -ㅂ시다, -ㄹ까요" ishlatib boʻlmaydi. "바빠서 나중에 오세요" notoʻgʻri.

column1: Don't put "-았/었-" before "-아서". Not "아팠어서" but "아파서 못 갔어요". With "-(으)니까" it's OK: "먹었으니까".
column2: -아서 dan oldin "-았/었-" qoʻymang. "아팠어서" emas, "아파서 못 갔어요". "-(으)니까" bilan mumkin: "먹었으니까".

Both can mean English "and then". If the two actions are separate, use "-고". If the first action leads into the second, use "-아서".

column2: Alohida harakatlar uchun "-고". Birinchi harakat ikkinchisiga olib kelsa, "-아서".

column2: 친구를 만나고 영화를 봤어요 — doʻstingiz bilan uchrashib, keyin ajralib, filmni yolgʻiz koʻrganingizni bildiradi. "만나서" esa birga koʻrganingizni bildiradi.

column1: A clear contrast uses "-지만". Soft linking or giving background uses "-는데".
column2: Aniq qarama-qarshilik uchun "-지만". Yumshoq bogʻlash yoki asos berish uchun "-는데".

column1: Before you ask or request something, first explain the situation with "-는데". It sounds polite: "길을 잘 모르는데 좀 가르쳐 주세요."
column2: Biror narsa soʻrash yoki iltimos qilishdan oldin vaziyatni "-는데" bilan tushuntiring. Bu odobli eshitiladi: "길을 잘 모르는데 좀 가르쳐 주세요."

column1: Verbs and "있다, 없다" use "-는데", adjectives use "-(으)ㄴ데", and nouns use "인데": 가는데, 없는데, 좋은데, 학생인데.
column2: Feʼllar va "있다, 없다" — "-는데", sifatlar — "-(으)ㄴ데", otlar esa "인데" bilan: 가는데, 없는데, 좋은데, 학생인데.

column1: Both mean English "will". "-(으)ㄹ게요" is a promise to the listener, and "-(으)ㄹ 거예요" is a plan or a guess.
column2: Ikkalasi ham kelasi zamonni bildiradi. "-(으)ㄹ게요" tinglovchiga beriladigan vaʼda, "-(으)ㄹ 거예요" esa reja yoki taxmin.

column1: A promise uses "-(으)ㄹ게요". Plans and guesses use "-(으)ㄹ 거예요".
column2: Vaʼda uchun "-(으)ㄹ게요". Rejalar va taxminlar uchun "-(으)ㄹ 거예요".

column1: -(으)ㄹ게요 is only used for "I, we", and you can't ask questions with it. "민하 씨가 할게요" and "할게요?" are wrong.
column2: -(으)ㄹ게요 faqat "men, biz" uchun ishlatiladi va u bilan savol berib boʻlmaydi. "민하 씨가 할게요" va "할게요?" notoʻgʻri.

column1: When you answer an order, use "-(으)ㄹ게요" or "-겠습니다": "이거 좀 해 줘요." "네, 할게요." Here "할 거예요" sounds unnatural.
column2: Buyruqqa javob berganda "-(으)ㄹ게요" yoki "-겠습니다" ishlating: "이거 좀 해 줘요." "네, 할게요." Bu yerda "할 거예요" gʻalati eshitiladi.

column1: If you don't do it, use "안". If you can't do it, use "못".

column1: With "noun + 하다" verbs, put it in the middle: "일 안 해요", "전화 못 해요". "안 일해요" is wrong.
column2: Ot + 하다 feʼllarida uni oʻrtaga qoʻying: "일 안 해요", "전화 못 해요". "안 일해요" notoʻgʻri.

Both are polite requests. "-(으)세요" suggests something for the listener, and "-아/어 주세요" asks someone to do something for me.
column2: Ikkalasi ham hurmatli iltimos. "-(으)세요" tinglovchiga biror narsani taklif qiladi, "-아/어 주세요" esa kimdandir men uchun biror narsa qilishni soʻraydi.

column1: Words for the listener's good use "-(으)세요". Requests for me use "-아/어 주세요".
column2: Tinglovchining foydasi uchun aytiladigan soʻzlarda "-(으)세요". Oʻzim uchun iltimoslarda "-아/어 주세요".

column1: When it helps you, say "-아/어 주세요". "문을 여세요" sounds like an order, and "문 좀 열어 주세요" is a request.
column2: Sizga foyda boʻlsa, "-아/어 주세요" deng. "문을 여세요" buyruqdek, "문 좀 열어 주세요" esa iltimosdek eshitiladi.

column1: When it's good for the listener, use "-(으)세요": "많이 드세요", "쉬세요", "조심하세요". Using "주세요" here sounds unnatural.
column2: Tinglovchi uchun yaxshi boʻlsa, "-(으)세요" ishlating: "많이 드세요", "쉬세요", "조심하세요". Bu yerda "주세요" ishlatish gʻalati eshitiladi.

please teach me, please tell me

Both are close to English "want to". "-고 싶다" is a wish in your heart, and "-(으)ㄹ래요" is choosing to do it now.
column2: Ikkalasi ham "xohlamoq" maʼnosiga yaqin. "-고 싶다" — yurakdagi istak, "-(으)ㄹ래요" esa hozir buni qilishni tanlash.

column1: Wishes use "-고 싶다". Choosing now and asking friends use "-(으)ㄹ래요".
column2: Istaklar uchun "-고 싶다". Hozir tanlash va doʻstlardan soʻrash uchun "-(으)ㄹ래요".

column1: -(으)ㄹ래요 is used between close people. "저는 쉴래요" sounds rude to someone above you. Use "쉬고 싶습니다" or "쉬어도 될까요?".
column2: -(으)ㄹ래요 yaqin odamlar orasida ishlatiladi. Yuqoridagi odamga "저는 쉴래요" desangiz, qoʻpol eshitiladi. "쉬고 싶습니다" yoki "쉬어도 될까요?" ishlating.

column1: When you ask what someone above you wants, use "-(으)시겠어요?": "뭐 드시겠어요?" Don't use "뭐 먹고 싶어요?" with people above you.
column2: Yuqoridagi odamdan nima xohlashini soʻraganda "-(으)시겠어요?" ishlating: "뭐 드시겠어요?" Yuqoridagi odamlarga "뭐 먹고 싶어요?" demang.

This is the difference between English "if" and "when". "-(으)면" is a condition that may or may not happen, and "-(으)ㄹ 때" is the time when it happens.
column2: Bu oʻzbekchadagi "-sa" (agar) va "-ganda" (... paytda) orasidagi farq. "-(으)면" boʻlishi ham, boʻlmasligi ham mumkin boʻlgan shart, "-(으)ㄹ 때" esa u sodir boʻladigan vaqt.

column1: A condition uses "-(으)면". The time when something happens uses "-(으)ㄹ 때".
column2: Shart uchun "-(으)면". Biror narsa sodir boʻladigan vaqt uchun "-(으)ㄹ 때".

column1: -(으)면 is also used for things that will surely happen. Then it means "when…": "방학이 되면 고향에 가요."
column2: -(으)면 albatta boʻladigan narsalar uchun ham ishlatiladi. Unda "...ganda" degan maʼnoni beradi: "방학이 되면 고향에 가요."

column1: For a time in the past, use "-았/었을 때": "한국에 처음 왔을 때 많이 힘들었어요."
column2: Oʻtgan zamondagi vaqt uchun "-았/었을 때" ishlating: "한국에 처음 왔을 때 많이 힘들었어요."

This is the polite ending used most in daily life. You can use it for what you are doing now, what you always do, and what you will do soon.
column2: Bu kundalik hayotda eng koʻp ishlatiladigan hurmatli qoʻshimcha. Uni hozir qilayotgan, doim qiladigan va tez orada qiladigan ishlaringiz uchun ishlatishingiz mumkin.

column1: After ㅏ, ㅗ use "-아요"; otherwise use "-어요"; 하다 becomes "해요".
column2: ㅏ, ㅗ dan keyin "-아요", boshqa hollarda "-어요" ishlating; 하다 esa 해요 boʻladi.

column1: Take off "-다". If the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, add "-아요"; for other vowels add "-어요"; "하다" becomes "해요". If the stem ends in a vowel, it shortens (가+아요 → 가요, 오+아요 → 와요, 마시+어요 → 마셔요, 배우+어요 → 배워요).
column2: -다 ni olib tashlang. Oxirgi unli ㅏ yoki ㅗ boʻlsa "-아요", boshqa unlilarda "-어요" qoʻshing; "하다" "해요" boʻladi. Oʻzak unli bilan tugasa, qisqaradi (가+아요 → 가요, 오+아요 → 와요, 마시+어요 → 마셔요, 배우+어요 → 배워요).

column1: English verbs change only a little (go, goes, went), but the endings of Korean verbs change in many ways. In the dictionary, they appear in the "-다" form.
column2: Oʻzbekchadagi kabi, koreys feʼllarining qoʻshimchalari koʻp xil oʻzgaradi. Lugʻatda ular "-다" shaklida beriladi (oʻzbekchadagi "-moq" kabi).

column1: The same form is used to tell, ask, tell someone to do something, and suggest doing it together: 가요. 가요? 빨리 가요! 같이 가요.
column2: Bir xil shakl xabar berish, soʻrash, buyurish va birga qilishni taklif qilish uchun ishlatiladi: 가요. 가요? 빨리 가요! 같이 가요.

column1: This is the formal ending used in official situations. It is used in meetings, presentations, interviews, announcements and the news.
column2: Bu rasmiy vaziyatlarda ishlatiladigan rasmiy qoʻshimcha. U yigʻilishlar, taqdimotlar, ish suhbatlari, eʼlonlar va yangiliklarda ishlatiladi.

column1: With a final consonant use "-습니다"; without one use "-ㅂ니다".
With a final consonant add "-습니다"; without one add "-ㅂ니다". To ask, use "-습니까?/ㅂ니까?".
column2: Oxirgi undosh boʻlsa "-습니다", boʻlmasa "-ㅂ니다" qoʻshing. Soʻrash uchun "-습니까?/ㅂ니까?" ishlating.
ㅂ니다 [ㅁ니다] deb talaffuz qilinadi: 갑니다 [감니다] (gamnida), 먹습니다 [먹씀니다] (meokseumnida).

column1: The ㄹ final consonant drops: 알다 → 압니다, 만들다 → 만듭니다.
column2: Oxirgi ㄹ tushib qoladi: 알다 → 압니다, 만들다 → 만듭니다.

column1: When answering a professor or a customer, "네, 알겠습니다", "감사합니다" and "죄송합니다" are always said in this style.
column2: Domla yoki mijozga javob berganda "네, 알겠습니다", "감사합니다" va "죄송합니다" doim shu uslubda aytiladi.

column1: I study business administration at Jeonju University.
column2: Men Chonju universitetida biznes boshqaruvini oʻqiyman.

I look forward to working with you. / Please treat me well.
column2: Hamkorlikdan umidvorman. / Iltimos, menga yaxshi munosabatda boʻling.

column1: Sam, is life in Korea OK for you?
Yes, it's fine. My friends help me a lot.
column2: Ha, yaxshi. Doʻstlarim koʻp yordam berishadi.

column1: to be fine, to be OK
If you have any difficulties, please tell me.
Used to speak or ask politely about what the listener or a respected person does.
column2: Tinglovchi yoki hurmatli odam qiladigan ish haqida hurmat bilan gapirish yoki soʻrash uchun ishlatiladi.

column1: Use "-(으)세요" to show respect for what other people do. Don't use it for yourself.
column2: Boshqa odamlar qiladigan ishlarga hurmat koʻrsatish uchun "-(으)세요" ishlating. Oʻzingiz uchun ishlatmang.

column1: With a final consonant add "-으세요"; without one add "-세요". It is a short form of "-(으)시- + -어요".
column2: Oxirgi undosh boʻlsa "-으세요", boʻlmasa "-세요" qoʻshing. Bu "-(으)시- + -어요" ning qisqa shakli.

column1: Don't use it for things you do yourself. If someone asks "어디 가세요?", answer "집에 가요". Saying "집에 가세요" is wrong.
column2: Oʻzingiz qiladigan ishlar uchun ishlatmang. Kimdir "어디 가세요?" deb soʻrasa, "집에 가요" deb javob bering. "집에 가세요" deyish notoʻgʻri.

column1: Some words change completely: 먹다 → 드세요, 자다 → 주무세요, 있다 (a person is somewhere) → 계세요.
column2: Baʼzi soʻzlar butunlay oʻzgaradi: 먹다 → 드세요, 자다 → 주무세요, 있다 (odam biror joyda boʻlsa) → 계세요.

column1: The same form is also used to tell someone politely to do something (앉으세요). You will learn this in H-01.
column2: Bir xil shakl kimgadir hurmat bilan biror narsa qilishni aytish uchun ham ishlatiladi (앉으세요). Buni H-01 da oʻrganasiz.

column1: The professor is having a meal now.
I'm going to the department office. What are you doing, Sam?
column2: Kafedra idorasiga ketyapman. Sam, siz nima qilyapsiz?

column1: I'm going to the library. Have you had lunch?
This marks respect for the subject of the sentence. Add it to the actions of older people, bosses, customers and people you meet for the first time.
column2: Bu gap egasiga hurmatni bildiradi. Uni katta yoshdagilar, boshliqlar, mijozlar va birinchi uchrashgan odamlarning harakatlariga qoʻshing.

column1: For the actions of a respected person, put "-(으)시-" in the verb.
column2: Hurmatli odamning harakatlari uchun feʼlga "-(으)시-" qoʻying.

column1: With a final consonant put in "-으시-"; without one put in "-시-", then add the ending: 가다 → 가십니다, 가셨어요, 가실 거예요.
column2: Oxirgi undosh boʻlsa "-으시-", boʻlmasa "-시-" qoʻyib, keyin qoʻshimchani qoʻshing: 가다 → 가십니다, 가셨어요, 가실 거예요.

column1: In English you show respect with words like "sir" or "please", but in Korean you put "-시-" inside the verb.
column2: Oʻzbekchada hurmat "-lar" qoʻshimchasi yoki "siz" bilan ifodalanadi (Domla keldilar), koreyschada esa feʼl ichiga "-시-" qoʻyiladi.

column1: The respect is for the person who does the action. Even if you are talking to a friend, when you talk about the professor you say "교수님이 오셨어".
column2: Hurmat harakatni bajaruvchi odamga qaratiladi. Doʻstingiz bilan gaplashayotgan boʻlsangiz ham, domla haqida "교수님이 오셨어" deysiz.

column1: The head of the department is in class.
She is in class now. It will finish in 30 minutes.
column2: U kishi hozir darsdalar. 30 daqiqadan keyin tugaydi.

column1: This is the respectful form of "이/가". Use it when a respected person is the subject.
column2: Bu "이/가" ning hurmat shakli. Hurmatli odam ega boʻlganda ishlating.

column1: When a respected person is the subject, use "께서" together with "-(으)시-".
column2: Hurmatli odam ega boʻlganda "께서" ni "-(으)시-" bilan birga ishlating.

column1: Add it after a person and also use "-(으)시-" in the verb. The respectful form of "은/는" is "께서는", and of "도" is "께서도".
column2: Uni odamdan keyin qoʻshib, feʼlda ham "-(으)시-" ishlating. "은/는" ning hurmat shakli "께서는", "도" niki esa "께서도".

column1: 께서 is used in formal speech and writing. In everyday talk, you can just use "이/가" with "-시-", as in "어머니가 요리하세요".
column2: 께서 rasmiy nutq va yozuvda ishlatiladi. Kundalik suhbatda "어머니가 요리하세요" kabi shunchaki "이/가" ni "-시-" bilan ishlatish mumkin.

column1: It is used with respectful words: 말 → 말씀, 집 → 댁, 나이 → 연세, 이름 → 성함, 밥 → 진지, 아프다 → 편찮으시다.
column2: U hurmat soʻzlari bilan ishlatiladi: 말 → 말씀, 집 → 댁, 나이 → 연세, 이름 → 성함, 밥 → 진지, 아프다 → 편찮으시다.

column1: The head of the department said so.
the head of the department (respectful, subject)

This is casual speech used with close friends, younger people and family. At work, older or senior people may also use it with junior people.
column2: Bu yaqin doʻstlar, yoshi kichiklar va oila bilan ishlatiladigan norasmiy nutq. Ishda katta yoshli yoki yuqori lavozimdagilar ham uni quyi lavozimdagilarga ishlatishi mumkin.

column1: Casual speech is "-아요/어요" without "요", and you use it only with people you are close to.
column2: Norasmiy nutq — "요" siz "-아요/어요", uni faqat yaqin odamlaringiz bilan ishlatasiz.

column1: Take "요" off "-아요/어요". "이에요/예요" becomes "이야/야". "네" becomes "응", and "아니요" becomes "아니".
column2: -아요/어요 dan "요" ni olib tashlang. "이에요/예요" "이야/야" ga aylanadi. "네" "응", "아니요" esa "아니" boʻladi.

column1: First, learn to understand casual speech. Use it yourself only after the other person says "말 편하게 해요" or "말 놓으세요" (You can speak casually).
column2: Avval norasmiy nutqni tushunishni oʻrganing. Uni oʻzingiz faqat suhbatdoshingiz "말 편하게 해요" yoki "말 놓으세요" (Bemalol "sen"lab gapiravering) deganidan keyin ishlating.

column1: Even if an older student (선배) or an older friend speaks casually to you, answer with "-요". Often they do not mean to be rude.
column2: Katta kursdosh (선배) yoki yoshi katta doʻstingiz siz bilan norasmiy gapirsa ham, "-요" bilan javob bering. Koʻpincha ular qoʻpollik qilmoqchi emas.

column1: Some verbs don't add "-(으)시-" to show respect; they use a completely different word. It is a bit like English using "dine" instead of "eat".
column2: Baʼzi feʼllar hurmat bildirish uchun "-(으)시-" qoʻshmaydi, butunlay boshqa soʻz ishlatadi. Bu oʻzbekchada "yemoq" oʻrniga "tanovul qilmoq" deyilganga biroz oʻxshaydi.

column1: Don't use these for yourself. To "많이 드세요", answer "네, 많이 먹겠습니다". "드시겠습니다" is wrong.
column2: Bularni oʻzingiz uchun ishlatmang. "많이 드세요" ga "네, 많이 먹겠습니다" deb javob bering. "드시겠습니다" notoʻgʻri.

column1: 안녕히 가세요 is said to the person leaving, and "안녕히 계세요" to the person staying.
column2: 안녕히 가세요 ketayotgan odamga, "안녕히 계세요" esa qolayotgan odamga aytiladi.

column1: 있다 has two honorific forms. When a person "is (somewhere)", use "계시다"; when someone "has" something, use "있으시다": "시간 있으세요?"
column2: 있다 ning ikkita hurmat shakli bor. Odam "biror joyda boʻlsa" "계시다", kimdadir biror narsa "bor boʻlsa" "있으시다" ishlating: "시간 있으세요?"

column1: Please eat a lot. (Enjoy your meal.)

When the professor is speaking, take notes.

column2: Professor Im Hyeonjeong kasal boʻlganlari uchun bugun dars yoʻq.

column1: Did you have lunch? (to the TA)

column2: Yoʻq, bugun kasal boʻlganlari uchun kelmadilar.

column1: These words make your own action toward an older or higher person humble, to show respect. The person you respect is the one who receives the action.
column2: Bu soʻzlar yoshi katta yoki yuqori lavozimdagi odamga qaratilgan oʻz harakatingizni kamtarona ifodalab, hurmat koʻrsatadi. Hurmat qilinadigan odam harakatni qabul qiluvchidir.

column1: For your actions toward older or higher people, use "드리다, 여쭙다, 뵙다, 모시다, 말씀드리다".
column2: Yoshi katta yoki yuqori lavozimdagi odamlarga qaratilgan harakatlaringiz uchun "드리다, 여쭙다, 뵙다, 모시다, 말씀드리다" ishlating.

column1: Use the two kinds of respect correctly. For what an older person does, use "-(으)시-" (교수님이 주셨어요); for what you do for an older person, use the humble word (교수님께 드렸어요).
column2: Ikki xil hurmatni toʻgʻri ishlating. Katta odam qiladigan ish uchun "-(으)시-" (교수님이 주셨어요), siz katta odam uchun qiladigan ish uchun kamtarlik soʻzi (교수님께 드렸어요).

column1: -아/어 주다 also becomes "-아/어 드리다". In restaurants and shops you often hear "해 드릴게요" and "가져다드리겠습니다".
column2: -아/어 주다 ham "-아/어 드리다" ga aylanadi. Oshxona va doʻkonlarda "해 드릴게요" va "가져다드리겠습니다" ni koʻp eshitasiz.

column1: to give (to an older or higher person)

On the holiday, I gave the professor some Greek coffee.
column2: Bayramda domlaga yunon kofesi sovgʻa qildim.

I'll see you at the interview tomorrow.

column1: I took the guest to the hotel.
I live with my parents and take care of them.
column2: Ota-onam bilan yashab, ularga gʻamxoʻrlik qilaman.

column1: Please take the guest to the department office.
I have something to tell you.
to give (humble) (드릴 말씀 = something to tell you)

column2: Domlaga kasal boʻlganim uchun darsga kelmasligimni aytdim.

column2: Bular yoshi katta yoki yuqori lavozimdagi odamlarga oid narsalar haqida gapirganda ishlatiladigan hurmat otlari.

column1: If you use an honorific noun, use an honorific verb too. "이름이 뭐예요?" (normal), "성함이 어떻게 되세요?" (honorific).
column2: Hurmat otini ishlatsangiz, hurmat feʼlini ham ishlating. "이름이 뭐예요?" (oddiy), "성함이 어떻게 되세요?" (hurmat).

column1: 진지 is used for elders in the family; at school and in shops use "식사". "식사하셨어요?" (Have you eaten?) is a Korean greeting.
column2: 진지 oiladagi kattalar uchun ishlatiladi; maktab va doʻkonlarda "식사" ishlating. "식사하셨어요?" (Ovqatlandingizmi?) — koreyscha salomlashish.

May I ask how old you are?

I was invited to the professor's house.

column2: Men Park Minhaman. Professor Sim Yeonggukni koʻrgani keldim.

column1: Yes, I'll let the professor know. Please wait here for a moment.
column2: Xoʻp, domlaga xabar beraman. Shu yerda biroz kutib turing.

column1: Korean shows respect to the listener by using a humble word for "I". English has no humble form of "I", so practice "저" carefully.
column2: Koreys tilida tinglovchiga hurmat "men" uchun kamtarlik soʻzini ishlatish orqali koʻrsatiladi. Oʻzbek tilida "men" ning kamtarlik shakli yoʻq, shuning uchun "저" ni yaxshilab mashq qiling.

column1: In front of older or higher people, use "저, 제가, 제, 저희" instead of "나, 내가, 내, 우리".
column2: Yoshi katta yoki yuqori lavozimdagilar oldida "나, 내가, 내, 우리" oʻrniga "저, 제가, 제, 저희" ishlating.

column1: When you speak with "-요" or "-습니다", use "저". "나는 샘입니다" sounds strange.
column2: -요 yoki "-습니다" bilan gapirganda "저" ishlating. "나는 샘입니다" gʻalati eshitiladi.

column1: When you talk about your school or shop to guests, say "저희 학교, 저희 가게". But you don't lower your country; say "우리나라".
column2: Mehmonlarga maktabingiz yoki doʻkoningiz haqida gapirganda "저희 학교, 저희 가게" deng. Lekin davlatingizni kamsitmaysiz; "우리나라" deng.

column1: to do wrong, to make a mistake

In Korean, the same greeting has three speech styles depending on the listener: formal (-습니다), soft polite (-요) and casual (반말).
column2: Koreys tilida bir xil salomlashish tinglovchiga qarab uch xil nutq uslubida aytiladi: rasmiy (-습니다), yumshoq hurmatli (-요) va norasmiy (반말).

column1: Greetings have three levels: formal "-습니다", soft "-요", and casual.
column2: Salomlashishning uch darajasi bor: rasmiy "-습니다", yumshoq "-요" va norasmiy.

column1: English "hello" is the same for everyone, but in Korean the form changes with the listener. If you are not sure which to use, use "-요".
column2: Oʻzbekchadagi "Assalomu alaykum" va "Salom" kabi, koreyschada ham shakl tinglovchiga qarab oʻzgaradi. Qaysi birini ishlatishni bilmasangiz, "-요" ni ishlating.

column1: To older or higher people, "미안해요, 고마워요" sounds too light. Use "죄송합니다, 감사합니다".
column2: Yoshi katta yoki yuqori lavozimdagilarga "미안해요, 고마워요" juda yengil eshitiladi. "죄송합니다, 감사합니다" ishlating.

column1: 안녕 is used both when meeting and when leaving, but only with friends and younger people.
column2: 안녕 uchrashganda ham, xayrlashganda ham ishlatiladi, lekin faqat doʻstlar va yoshi kichiklar bilan.

column1: Hello. I'm Sam, and I'm taking this class from today.
column2: Assalomu alaykum. Men Samman, bugundan boshlab shu darsda qatnashaman.

Hello. I just moved to this floor.
column2: Assalomu alaykum. Men shu qavatga yangi koʻchib keldim.
Xayr! Dam olish kunlaringni yaxshi oʻtkaz!

column1: Thank you so much for interpreting.
column2: Tarjima qilib berganingiz uchun katta rahmat.

column2: Oh, Sam. Salom. Dars sizga maqulmi?

Questions also have three speech styles. If the listener is older or higher, also add "-(으)시-".
column2: Savollar ham uch xil nutq uslubiga ega. Tinglovchi yoshi katta yoki yuqori lavozimda boʻlsa, "-(으)시-" ni ham qoʻshing.

column1: When you ask older or higher people, use "-(으)세요?" or "-(으)십니까?".
column2: Yoshi katta yoki yuqori lavozimdagilardan soʻraganda "-(으)세요?" yoki "-(으)십니까?" ishlating.

column1: When you ask about what an older or higher person does, don't just change the ending; add "-(으)시-". Say "어디 가세요?", not "어디 가요?".
column2: Yoshi katta yoki yuqori odam qiladigan ish haqida soʻraganda faqat qoʻshimchani oʻzgartirmang; "-(으)시-" ni qoʻshing. "어디 가요?" emas, "어디 가세요?" deng.

column1: 어디 가세요? and "식사하셨어요?" are greetings. You don't need to answer in detail: "네, 잠깐 나가요", "네, 먹었습니다".
column2: 어디 가세요? va "식사하셨어요?" — salomlashuvlar. Batafsil javob berish shart emas: "네, 잠깐 나가요", "네, 먹었습니다".

column1: Where are you going? I'll take you there.
Professor, where are you going? Shall I carry your bag?
column2: Domla, qayerga ketyapsiz? Sumkangizni koʻtarib beraymi?

Where are you going at this hour?

Requests and instructions also have three speech styles. The more polite a request is, the longer it gets.
column2: Iltimos va koʻrsatmalar ham uch xil nutq uslubiga ega. Iltimos qanchalik hurmatli boʻlsa, shunchalik uzun boʻladi.

column1: Requests get more polite in this order: "줘 → 주세요 → 주십시오 → 주시겠어요?".
column2: Iltimoslar shu tartibda hurmatliroq boʻladi: "줘 → 주세요 → 주십시오 → 주시겠어요?".

column1: When you ask an older or higher person, a question form is more polite than an order form: "-아/어 주시겠어요?", "-아/어 주실 수 있으세요?"
column2: Yoshi katta yoki yuqori odamdan soʻraganda savol shakli buyruq shaklidan hurmatliroq: "-아/어 주시겠어요?", "-아/어 주실 수 있으세요?"

column1: Adding "죄송하지만", "실례지만" or "바쁘시겠지만" (I know you're busy, but…) before a request makes it softer.
column2: Iltimosdan oldin "죄송하지만", "실례지만" yoki "바쁘시겠지만" (Band ekaningizni bilaman, lekin…) qoʻshish uni yumshoqroq qiladi.

column1: Could you say that again, please?
column2: Buni yana bir bor ayta olasizmi?

column1: Could you close the window, please?
Could you say it again slowly, please?
Excuse me, but please help me.
I can't read this Korean document. Please help me.

column1: Answers also change with the speech style. In class and at a part-time job, it is important to answer clearly.
column2: Javoblar ham nutq uslubiga qarab oʻzgaradi. Darsda va ishda aniq javob berish muhim.

column1: To older or higher people answer "네, 알겠습니다"; if you didn't understand, say "잘 못 들었습니다".
column2: Yoshi katta yoki yuqori odamlarga "네, 알겠습니다" deb javob bering; tushunmasangiz "잘 못 들었습니다" deng.

column1: Answering an older or higher person with "응" or "어" is very rude. Always say "네" or "예".
column2: Yoshi katta yoki yuqori odamga "응" yoki "어" deb javob berish juda qoʻpol. Doim "네" yoki "예" deng.

column1: Don't say "네" if you didn't understand. Say "죄송합니다. 잘 못 들었습니다" or "다시 한번 말씀해 주십시오". Saying "네" when you don't understand causes problems later.
column2: Tushunmasangiz "네" demang. "죄송합니다. 잘 못 들었습니다" yoki "다시 한번 말씀해 주십시오" deng. Tushunmay turib "네" deyish keyinchalik muammolarga olib keladi.

column1: 네 means not only "yes" but is also used to show "I'm listening". It is also the answer when someone calls your name: "샘 씨!" "네!"
column2: 네 nafaqat "ha" degani, balki "tinglayapman" deb bildirish uchun ham ishlatiladi. Kimdir ismingizni chaqirganda ham shunday javob beriladi: "샘 씨!" "네!"

column1: No. I'm not the one who did it.

Take this coffee to table 3 and give it to the customer. Got it?

column2: Kechirasiz. Qaysi stol ekanini eshitmay qoldim.

column1: This is practice changing words with the same meaning for different listeners. The speech style depends on age, your relationship and how close you are.
column2: Bu bir xil maʼnoli soʻzlarni turli tinglovchilarga qarab oʻzgartirish mashqi. Nutq uslubi yosh, munosabat va qanchalik yaqinligingizga bogʻliq.

column1: Use the formal style with professors and guests, "-요" with seniors and new classmates, and casual speech only with close friends.
column2: Domlalar va mehmonlar bilan rasmiy uslubni, katta kursdoshlar va yangi kursdoshlar bilan "-요" ni, faqat yaqin doʻstlar bilan norasmiy nutqni ishlating.

column1: With people you meet for the first time, use "-요" whatever their age. Use casual speech only after the other person says "말 편하게 해요".
column2: Birinchi marta uchrashgan odamlar bilan yoshidan qatʼi nazar "-요" ishlating. Norasmiy nutqni faqat suhbatdoshingiz "말 편하게 해요" deganidan keyin ishlating.

column1: At Korean universities, who entered first (학번, entry year) often matters more than age. Even if they are younger, use polite speech with seniors.
column2: Koreya universitetlarida kim oldin oʻqishga kirgani (학번, kirish yili) koʻpincha yoshdan muhimroq. Yoshi kichik boʻlsa ham, katta kursdoshlar bilan hurmat shaklida gapiring.

good work (said to someone younger or lower)

to work hard (수고하셨습니다 = thank you for your hard work)

Used to talk about the past. English uses a past form of the verb (worked, went); Korean puts "-았/었-" in the verb.
column2: Oʻtgan zamon haqida gapirish uchun ishlatiladi. Oʻzbekchadagi "-di" (ishladi, bordi) kabi, koreyschada feʼlga "-았/었-" qoʻyiladi.

column1: For past events, put "-았/었-" in the verb.
It follows the same rule as "-아요/어요". After ㅏ, ㅗ use "-았어요"; otherwise use "-었어요"; 하다 becomes "했어요". For nouns use "이었어요/였어요".
column2: U "-아요/어요" bilan bir xil qoidaga boʻysunadi. ㅏ, ㅗ dan keyin "-았어요", boshqa hollarda "-었어요" ishlating; 하다 "했어요" boʻladi. Otlar uchun "이었어요/였어요" ishlating.

column1: Even with words like "어제", you must change the verb. "어제 가요" is wrong; "어제 갔어요" is right. (Just like "Yesterday I go" is wrong in English.)
column2: 어제 kabi soʻzlar bilan ham feʼlni oʻzgartirish shart. "어제 가요" notoʻgʻri, "어제 갔어요" toʻgʻri. (Xuddi oʻzbekchada "Kecha boraman" notoʻgʻri boʻlgani kabi.)

column1: The formal form is "-았습니다/었습니다": 했습니다, 갔습니다.
아직 안 했어요 means "I haven't done it yet", and "벌써 했어요" means "I already did it".
column2: 아직 안 했어요 — "Hali qilmadim", "벌써 했어요" esa "Allaqachon qildim" degani.

column1: I came to Korea last year.
Sam, why didn't you come to class yesterday?
I'm sorry. I was very sick.
Did you go to the hospital?
Yes, I did. I took medicine too.
Used to talk about things you will do or plans. It is like "will, be going to" in English. It is also used for guesses (probably will).
column2: Qiladigan ishlar yoki rejalar haqida gapirish uchun ishlatiladi. Oʻzbekchadagi "-aman, -moqchiman" kabi. Taxmin uchun ham ishlatiladi (… boʻlsa kerak).

column1: Talk about things you will do with "-(으)ㄹ 거예요".
column2: Qiladigan ishlaringiz haqida "-(으)ㄹ 거예요" bilan gapiring.

column1: With a final consonant add "-을 거예요"; without one add "-ㄹ 거예요". With a ㄹ final consonant, just add "거예요".
column2: Oxirgi undosh boʻlsa "-을 거예요", boʻlmasa "-ㄹ 거예요" qoʻshing. Oxirgi undosh ㄹ boʻlsa, shunchaki "거예요" qoʻshing.

column1: In English, "will" comes before the verb, but in Korean it is added after it: "will go" = "갈 거예요".
column2: Oʻzbekchadagi kabi, u feʼldan keyin qoʻshiladi: "boraman" = "갈 거예요".

column1: 거예요 is pronounced [꺼예요]: 갈 거예요 [갈 꺼예요] (gal kkeoyeyo).
column2: 거예요 [꺼예요] deb talaffuz qilinadi: 갈 거예요 [갈 꺼예요] (gal kkeoyeyo).

column1: The formal form is "-(으)ㄹ 것입니다, -(으)ㄹ 겁니다".
What will you do on the weekend?
I'm going to my hometown next year.
What will you do this vacation?
I'm going to Nepal. I will see my family.
That's great. When will you come back?
I'll come back in two weeks.
Tells what you are doing right now. It is like "be + -ing" in English.
column2: Hozir nima qilayotganingizni aytadi. Oʻzbekchadagi "-yapti" (qilyapman) kabi.

column1: Take "-다" off the verb and add "-고 있어요". The final consonant does not matter. The respectful form is "-고 계세요".
column2: Feʼldan "-다" ni olib tashlab, "-고 있어요" qoʻshing. Oxirgi undosh ahamiyatsiz. Hurmat shakli "-고 계세요".

column1: In Korean, "-아요/어요" alone can also show what you are doing now. "뭐 해요?" and "뭐 하고 있어요?" are almost the same.
column2: Koreys tilida "-아요/어요" ning oʻzi ham hozir qilayotgan ishni bildirishi mumkin. "뭐 해요?" va "뭐 하고 있어요?" deyarli bir xil.

column1: Verbs for wearing also show the state of wearing something. "모자를 쓰고 있어요" means you are putting on a hat, or you are already wearing one.
column2: Kiyish feʼllari biror narsani kiyib turgan holatni ham bildiradi. "모자를 쓰고 있어요" — kepka kiyayotganingizni yoki allaqachon kiyib turganingizni bildiradi.

column1: I'm studying at the library now.
She's looking for a book in the library.
It has two meanings: ① the speaker's intention (will) ② a guess (must be, it seems). It is also found in many set greetings.
column2: U ikki maʼnoga ega: ① gapiruvchining niyati (qilaman) ② taxmin (shekilli, boʻlsa kerak). U koʻp tayyor salomlashuvlarda ham uchraydi.

column1: -겠- shows the speaker's intention and a guess.
Take "-다" off a verb or adjective, put in "-겠-", then add the ending. The final consonant does not matter.
column2: Feʼl yoki sifatdan "-다" ni olib tashlab, "-겠-" qoʻying, keyin qoʻshimchani qoʻshing. Oxirgi undosh ahamiyatsiz.

column1: 알겠습니다 is the most common answer when you get an instruction. "알아요" means "I already know", so it sounds rude as an answer to an instruction.
column2: 알겠습니다 — koʻrsatma olganda eng koʻp beriladigan javob. "알아요" "Men allaqachon bilaman" degani, shuning uchun koʻrsatmaga javob sifatida qoʻpol eshitiladi.

column1: Set greetings: 처음 뵙겠습니다 (Nice to meet you), 잘 먹겠습니다 (Thank you for the food), 다녀오겠습니다 (I'll be back), 실례하겠습니다 (Excuse me).
column2: Tayyor salomlashuvlar: 처음 뵙겠습니다 (Tanishganimdan xursandman), 잘 먹겠습니다 (Ovqat uchun rahmat), 다녀오겠습니다 (Borib kelaman), 실례하겠습니다 (Kechirasiz).

column1: Thank you for the food. (said before eating)
This assignment has to be handed in by today.
Yes, I understand. I'll do it.
It must be hard to do it alone. Do it with Aisha.
column2: Yolgʻiz qilish qiyin boʻlsa kerak. Aisha bilan birga qiling.

column1: It is used in two ways: ① to suggest trying something (try … and see) ② to talk about experience (have done).
column2: U ikki xil ishlatiladi: ① biror narsani sinab koʻrishni taklif qilish (…b koʻring) ② tajriba haqida gapirish (…gan).

column1: -아/어 보세요 means "try … and see", and "-아/어 봤어요" means "have (done)…".
Take "요" off the "-아요/어요" form and add "보다": 먹어 보세요 (try eating it), 먹어 봤어요 (I have eaten it).
column2: -아요/어요 shaklidan "요" ni olib tashlab, "보다" qoʻshing: 먹어 보세요 (yeb koʻring), 먹어 봤어요 (yeganman).

column1: The idea is the same as English "try … and see". "보다" means "see".
column2: Gʻoya oʻzbekchadagi "-b koʻrmoq" bilan bir xil. "보다" — "koʻrmoq" degani.

column1: 아직 안 해 봤어요 means "I haven't tried it yet".
column2: 아직 안 해 봤어요 — "Hali qilib koʻrmaganman" degani.

column1: Don't use it with "보다" itself. Don't say "봐 봤어요"; say "봤어요" or "본 적이 있어요".
column2: Uni "보다" ning oʻzi bilan ishlatmang. "봐 봤어요" demang; "봤어요" yoki "본 적이 있어요" deng.

column1: No, I haven't tried it yet.
Says whether you have or have not done something up to now. It is like "have ever (done)" in English.
column2: Hozirgacha biror narsani qilgan yoki qilmaganingizni aytadi. Oʻzbekchadagi "-gan" (borganman, koʻrmaganman) kabi.

column1: -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다/없다 means "have ever / have never".
With a final consonant add "-은 적이 있어요"; without one add "-ㄴ 적이 있어요". If you have not, use "-(으)ㄴ 적이 없어요".
column2: Oxirgi undosh boʻlsa "-은 적이 있어요", boʻlmasa "-ㄴ 적이 있어요" qoʻshing. Qilmagan boʻlsangiz, "-(으)ㄴ 적이 없어요" ishlating.

column1: In English, "have ever" comes before the verb, but in Korean it is added after it: "have been there" = "간 적이 있어요".
column2: Oʻzbekchadagi kabi, u feʼldan keyin qoʻshiladi: "borganman" = "간 적이 있어요".

column1: It is often asked in (part-time) job interviews: "아르바이트를 한 적이 있습니까?" (Have you ever had a part-time job?), "커피를 만들어 본 적이 있습니까?" (Have you ever made coffee?).
column2: Bu (qoʻshimcha) ish suhbatlarida koʻp soʻraladi: "아르바이트를 한 적이 있습니까?" (Qoʻshimcha ishda ishlaganmisiz?), "커피를 만들어 본 적이 있습니까?" (Kofe tayyorlaganmisiz?).

column1: Don't use it for things you do every day. "밥을 먹은 적이 있어요" sounds strange.
column2: Uni har kuni qiladigan ishlar uchun ishlatmang. "밥을 먹은 적이 있어요" gʻalati eshitiladi.

column1: I have worked part-time at a cafe.
Have you ever been to Korea?
Have you ever used this program?
Have you ever worked at a cafe?
Yes, I worked at one in the USA for a year.
Have you ever worked at a cafe in Korea?
No, I haven't. This is my first time.
안 means "not, don't". It means you don't do something or something is not so.
column2: 안 — "-ma, emas" degani. Biror narsani qilmasligingizni yoki biror narsa unday emasligini bildiradi.

column1: 안 + verb means "not + verb". "Noun + 하다" becomes "noun + 안 해요".
column2: 안 + feʼl — "feʼl + -ma" degani. "Ot + 하다" "ot + 안 해요" ga aylanadi.

column1: Put "안" right before the verb or adjective. With "noun + 하다" verbs, put it between the noun and "하다" (공부 안 해요).
column2: 안 ni feʼl yoki sifatdan bevosita oldin qoʻying. "Ot + 하다" feʼllarida uni ot va "하다" orasiga qoʻying (공부 안 해요).

column1: Like English "don't + verb", "안" comes before the verb, so it is easy. But the object comes before "안": "don't eat rice" = "밥을 안 먹어요".
column2: Oʻzbekchada inkor "-ma" qoʻshimchasi feʼldan keyin keladi, "안" esa feʼldan oldin keladi. Toʻldiruvchi "안" dan oldin keladi: "guruch yemayman" = "밥을 안 먹어요".

column1: For "있다" say "없어요", not "안 있어요"; for "알다" say "몰라요", not "안 알아요"; for "이다" say "아니에요".
column2: 있다 uchun "안 있어요" emas, "없어요"; "알다" uchun "안 알아요" emas, "몰라요"; "이다" uchun "아니에요" deng.

column1: I didn't work my part-time job yesterday.
It means "not", the same as "안". It is a little more formal and used a lot in writing.
column2: U "안" bilan bir xil "-ma, emas" maʼnosini beradi. Biroz rasmiyroq va yozuvda koʻp ishlatiladi.

column1: -지 않다 means the same as "안" and is more formal.
column2: -지 않다 "안" bilan bir xil maʼnoda, lekin rasmiyroq.

column1: Take "-다" off a verb or adjective and add "-지 않아요". The final consonant does not matter.
column2: Feʼl yoki sifatdan "-다" ni olib tashlab, "-지 않아요" qoʻshing. Oxirgi undosh ahamiyatsiz.

column1: 않아요 is pronounced [아나요] (anayo). The ㅎ is silent.
column2: 않아요 [아나요] (anayo) deb talaffuz qilinadi. ㅎ aytilmaydi.

column1: For the past, change "않다": "-지 않았어요". "갔지 않아요" is wrong.
column2: Oʻtgan zamon uchun "않다" ni oʻzgartiring: "-지 않았어요". "갔지 않아요" notoʻgʻri.

column1: With long words or "noun + 하다", "-지 않다" sounds more natural: "필요하지 않아요".
column2: Uzun soʻzlar yoki "ot + 하다" bilan "-지 않다" tabiiyroq eshitiladi: "필요하지 않아요".

column1: 못 means you want to do something but cannot. It is like "can't" in English.
column2: 못 biror narsani qilishni xohlasangiz ham qila olmasligingizni bildiradi. Oʻzbekchadagi "-a olmaslik" ga oʻxshaydi.

column1: Put it right before the verb. "Noun + 하다" becomes "noun + 못 해요".
column2: Uni feʼldan bevosita oldin qoʻying. "Ot + 하다" "ot + 못 해요" ga aylanadi.

column1: Like English "can't", "못" comes before the verb: "can't go" = "못 가요".
column2: 못 feʼldan oldin keladi: "bora olmayman" = "못 가요".

column1: 안 가요 means you don't go because you don't want to; "못 가요" means you can't go because of some reason. When saying no, "못 가요" sounds softer.
column2: 안 가요 — xohlamaganingiz uchun bormasligingizni, "못 가요" esa biror sabab bilan bora olmasligingizni bildiradi. Rad etganda "못 가요" yumshoqroq eshitiladi.

column1: The sound changes: 못 해요 [모태요] (motaeyo), 못 먹어요 [몬머거요] (monmeogeoyo), 못 가요 [몯까요] (motkkayo).
column2: Tovush oʻzgaradi: 못 해요 [모태요] (motaeyo), 못 먹어요 [몬머거요] (monmeogeoyo), 못 가요 [몯까요] (motkkayo).

column1: I was sick yesterday, so I couldn't go.
column2: Kecha kasal boʻlganim uchun bora olmadim.

column1: I'm not good at Korean yet.
to be bad at, can't do well
It means the same as "못". It is a little more formal and used a lot in writing.
column2: U "못" bilan bir xil maʼnoni beradi. Biroz rasmiyroq va yozuvda koʻp ishlatiladi.

column1: -지 못하다 means the same as "못" and is more formal.
column2: -지 못하다 "못" bilan bir xil maʼnoda, lekin rasmiyroq.

column1: Take "-다" off the verb and add "-지 못해요".
column2: Feʼldan "-다" ni olib tashlab, "-지 못해요" qoʻshing.

column1: It is often used when you hand in an assignment late or apologize: "죄송합니다. 끝내지 못했습니다." (I'm sorry. I couldn't finish it.)
column2: U topshiriqni kech topshirganda yoki uzr soʻraganda koʻp ishlatiladi: "죄송합니다. 끝내지 못했습니다." (Kechirasiz. Tugata olmadim.)

column1: It is usually not used with adjectives. Don't say "춥지 못해요"; say "춥지 않아요".
column2: Odatda sifatlar bilan ishlatilmaydi. "춥지 못해요" demang; "춥지 않아요" deng.

column1: I couldn't finish all the assignment.
Sam, did you finish writing the report?
I'm sorry. I haven't finished it yet.
My laptop broke down, so I couldn't write it yesterday.
column2: Noutbukim buzilib qolgani uchun kecha yoza olmadim.

column1: to happen, to occur (고장 나다 = to break down)
Says whether you are able to, or have the chance to, do something. It is like "can / can't" in English.
column2: Biror narsani qila olish yoki qila olmasligingizni, imkoniyatingiz borligini aytadi. Oʻzbekchadagi "-a olmoq / -a olmaslik" ga oʻxshaydi.

column1: -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 means "can", and "-(으)ㄹ 수 없다" means "can't".
column2: -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 — "...a olaman", "-(으)ㄹ 수 없다" esa "...a olmayman" degani.

column1: With a final consonant add "-을 수 있어요"; without one add "-ㄹ 수 있어요".
column2: Oxirgi undosh boʻlsa "-을 수 있어요", boʻlmasa "-ㄹ 수 있어요" qoʻshing.

column1: In English, "can" comes before the verb, but in Korean "수 있어요" comes at the end: "can do" = "할 수 있어요".
column2: Oʻzbekchadagi kabi, "수 있어요" oxirida keladi: "qila olaman" = "할 수 있어요".

column1: 수 is pronounced [쑤]: 할 수 있어요 [할 쑤 이써요] (hal ssu isseoyo).
column2: 수 [쑤] deb talaffuz qilinadi: 할 수 있어요 [할 쑤 이써요] (hal ssu isseoyo).

column1: For skills you have learned, you can also say "-(으)ㄹ 줄 알아요/몰라요": "운전할 줄 알아요." (I know how to drive.)
column2: Oʻrgangan koʻnikmalaringiz uchun "-(으)ㄹ 줄 알아요/몰라요" ham deyish mumkin: "운전할 줄 알아요." (Mashina haydashni bilaman.)

column1: Can I use a card here?
column2: Bu yerda karta bilan toʻlasa boʻladimi?

column1: Yes, I can speak a little.
Can you work on weekends too?
column2: Dam olish kunlari ham ishlay olasizmi?

column1: No, I can't on weekends. I can work on weekday evenings.
column2: Yoʻq, dam olish kunlari ishlay olmayman. Ish kunlari kechqurun ishlay olaman.

column1: Says what you want to do. It is like "want to" in English.
column2: Nima qilishni xohlashingizni aytadi. Oʻzbekchadagi "-gim keladi, -moqchiman" ga oʻxshaydi.

column1: Take "-다" off the verb and add "-고 싶어요". The final consonant does not matter.
column2: Feʼldan "-다" ni olib tashlab, "-고 싶어요" qoʻshing. Oxirgi undosh ahamiyatsiz.

column1: In English, "want to" comes before the verb, but in Korean it is added after it: "want to go" = "가고 싶어요".
column2: Oʻzbekchadagi kabi, u feʼldan keyin qoʻshiladi: "borgim keladi" = "가고 싶어요".

column1: Use it only for your own wishes and the listener's. For other people's wishes, use "-고 싶어 해요": "동생이 한국에 오고 싶어 해요." (My younger brother wants to come to Korea.)
column2: Uni faqat oʻzingiz va tinglovchining istaklari uchun ishlating. Boshqa odamlarning istaklari uchun "-고 싶어 해요" ishlating: "동생이 한국에 오고 싶어 해요." (Ukam Koreyaga kelmoqchi.)

column1: 보고 싶어요 is often used to mean "I miss (you)".
column2: 보고 싶어요 koʻpincha "(Sizni) sogʻindim" maʼnosida ishlatiladi.

column1: I want to work at a hotel.
to see (보고 싶다 = to miss, want to see)
I don't want to do anything today.
Sam, what do you want to do after graduation?
column2: Sam, oʻqishni bitirgandan keyin nima qilmoqchisiz?

column1: I want to work at a hotel. And I want to help my family.
column2: Mehmonxonada ishlamoqchiman. Oilamga ham yordam bermoqchiman.

column1: Which country do you want to work in?
Used to say casually what you will do, or to ask what the listener wants to do. It is used between people who are close.
column2: Nima qilishingizni oddiy aytish yoki tinglovchi nima qilmoqchi ekanini soʻrash uchun ishlatiladi. Yaqin odamlar orasida ishlatiladi.

column1: -(으)ㄹ래요 is used between close people to say what you want or to ask what the other person wants.
column2: -(으)ㄹ래요 yaqin odamlar orasida nima xohlashingizni aytish yoki suhbatdoshingiz nima xohlashini soʻrash uchun ishlatiladi.

column1: With a final consonant add "-을래요"; without one add "-ㄹ래요".
Don't use it to tell a senior person what you want. Saying "저는 갈래요" to a professor sounds rude. Say "가겠습니다".
column2: Katta odamga nima xohlashingizni aytish uchun ishlatmang. Domlaga "저는 갈래요" deyish qoʻpol eshitiladi. "가겠습니다" deng.

column1: To ask a senior person, use "-(으)시겠어요?": "뭐 드시겠어요?"
column2: Katta odamdan soʻrash uchun "-(으)시겠어요?" ishlating: "뭐 드시겠어요?"

column1: This is what you hear most when choosing food at a restaurant: "뭐 먹을래요?"
column2: Bu oshxonada taom tanlayotganda eng koʻp eshitiladigan ibora: "뭐 먹을래요?"

column1: What do you want to drink?
Do you want to go together?
Do you want to do it?
I'll have kimchi stew. And you, Minha?
column2: Men kimchi jjigae olaman. Siz-chi, Minha?

column1: I'll have soybean paste stew. Do you want a drink too?
column2: Men soya pastali shoʻrva olaman. Ichimlik ham olasizmi?

column1: Used when you promise the listener you will do something. It feels like "I'll … (for you)".
column2: Tinglovchiga biror narsa qilishni vaʼda qilganda ishlatiladi. "(Siz uchun) ... qilaman" degan maʼnoga yaqin.

column1: -(으)ㄹ게요 is a promise that you will do something.
With a final consonant add "-을게요"; without one add "-ㄹ게요". The subject is always "I".
column2: Oxirgi undosh boʻlsa "-을게요", boʻlmasa "-ㄹ게요" qoʻshing. Ega doim "men".

column1: It is not used in questions. "할게요?" is wrong.
-(으)ㄹ 거예요 is your own plan, and "-(으)ㄹ게요" is a promise made with the listener in mind: "내일 갈 거예요" (plan), "내일 갈게요" (promise).
column2: -(으)ㄹ 거예요 — oʻzingizning rejangiz, "-(으)ㄹ게요" esa tinglovchini hisobga olib beriladigan vaʼda: "내일 갈 거예요" (reja), "내일 갈게요" (vaʼda).

column1: I'll be going now. (I'm leaving first.)
Thank you for the food. (said when someone treats you)
column2: Ovqat uchun rahmat. (kimdir mehmon qilganda aytiladi)

column1: Who will take this box to the department office?
column2: Bu qutini kafedra idorasiga kim olib boradi?

column1: Thanks. It's heavy, so be careful.
column2: Rahmat. Ogʻir, shuning uchun ehtiyot boʻling.

column1: Used to suggest doing something together (Shall we …?) or to ask if you should do something (Shall I …?).
column2: Biror narsani birga qilishni taklif qilish (…aylikmi?) yoki biror narsani qilishim kerakmi deb soʻrash (…aymi?) uchun ishlatiladi.

column1: -(으)ㄹ까요? is used to suggest doing something together or to ask if you should do something.
column2: -(으)ㄹ까요? biror narsani birga qilishni taklif qilganda yoki biror narsani qilishim kerakmi deb soʻraganda ishlatiladi.

column1: With a final consonant add "-을까요?"; without one add "-ㄹ까요?".
Answer with "네, 좋아요", "-(으)ㅂ시다" or "-아/어요". If you don't want to, say no softly, like "미안해요, 오늘은 좀…".
column2: 네, 좋아요, "-(으)ㅂ시다" yoki "-아/어요" bilan javob bering. Agar xohlamasangiz, "미안해요, 오늘은 좀…" kabi yumshoq rad eting.

column1: 제가 ~(으)ㄹ까요? asks if there is something for you to do. At a part-time job or in a group project, people often ask "뭘 할까요?" (What shall I do?).
column2: 제가 ~(으)ㄹ까요? sizga qiladigan ish bormi deb soʻraydi. Qoʻshimcha ishda yoki guruh loyihasida koʻpincha "뭘 할까요?" (Nima qilay?) deb soʻrashadi.

column1: Shall we watch a movie together on the weekend?
column2: Dam olish kunlari birga kino koʻramizmi?

column1: Sounds good. Where shall we meet?
Shall we meet in front of the station at 2?
Used to suggest doing something together. It is like "Let's …" in English.
column2: Biror narsani birga qilishni taklif qilish uchun ishlatiladi. Oʻzbek tilidagi "…aylik" ga oʻxshaydi.

column1: -(으)ㅂ시다 means "Let's …", and it is not used with senior people.
column2: -(으)ㅂ시다 "…aylik" degan maʼnoni bildiradi va yoshi yoki mavqei kattalarga nisbatan ishlatilmaydi.

column1: With a final consonant add "-읍시다"; without one add "-ㅂ시다". The casual form is "-자".
column2: Oxirgi undosh boʻlsa "-읍시다", boʻlmasa "-ㅂ시다" qoʻshiladi. Norasmiy shakli "-자".

column1: Don't use it with senior people. To a professor, say "가시지요" or "같이 가시겠어요?".
column2: Yoshi yoki mavqei kattalarga ishlatmang. Professorga "가시지요" yoki "같이 가시겠어요?" deng.

column1: Professors and club leaders (선배) often use it when speaking to a group: "자, 시작합시다" (OK, let's start), "조용히 합시다" (Let's be quiet).
column2: Professorlar va togʻarak rahbarlari (선배) guruhga gapirganda koʻp ishlatadi: "자, 시작합시다" (Xoʻsh, boshladik), "조용히 합시다" (Jim boʻlaylik).

column1: In normal conversation, "-아요/어요" like "같이 가요" sounds softer.
column2: Oddiy suhbatda "같이 가요" kabi "-아요/어요" yumshoqroq eshitiladi.

column1: Everyone, let's finish today's practice here.
column2: Hammaga, bugungi mashgʻulotni shu yerda tugataylik.

column1: OK, thank you for your hard work.
Let's tidy up and go have dinner together.
Tells what you intend to do. It is like "plan to, be going to" in English.
column2: Nima qilmoqchi ekaningizni bildiradi. Oʻzbek tilidagi "-moqchiman, rejalashtiryapman" ga oʻxshaydi.

column1: With a final consonant add "-으려고 해요"; with no final consonant or a ㄹ final consonant add "-려고 해요".
column2: Oxirgi undosh boʻlsa "-으려고 해요", oxirgi undosh boʻlmasa yoki oxirgi undosh ㄹ boʻlsa "-려고 해요" qoʻshiladi.

column1: -(으)려고 했어요 often means you were going to do something but didn't.
column2: -(으)려고 했어요 koʻpincha biror narsa qilmoqchi edingiz, lekin qilmadingiz degan maʼnoni bildiradi.

column1: It is also used for something about to happen: "비가 오려고 해요" = It's about to rain.
column2: U yana yaqinda sodir boʻladigan narsa uchun ham ishlatiladi: "비가 오려고 해요" = Yomgʻir yogʻay deb turibdi.

column1: In speaking, it is shortened to "-(으)려고요": "어디 가요?" "은행에 가려고요." (Where are you going? To the bank.)
column2: Ogʻzaki nutqda u "-(으)려고요" ga qisqaradi: "어디 가요?" "은행에 가려고요." (Qayerga ketyapsiz? Bankka.)

column1: I plan to go to Korea next year.
I plan to rest at home on the weekend.
column2: Dam olish kunlari uyda dam olmoqchiman.

column1: I plan to save money and buy a laptop.
I was going to call, but I forgot.
column2: Qoʻngʻiroq qilmoqchi edim, lekin unutib qoʻydim.

column1: What will you do when you graduate?
I plan to go back to Myanmar and open a shop.
I plan to run a Korean restaurant.
It means you have agreed or promised to do something. It is like "decide to, agree to" in English.
column2: Biror narsa qilishga kelishganingiz yoki vaʼda berganingizni bildiradi. Oʻzbek tilidagi "…ishga qaror qildim, kelishdik" ga oʻxshaydi.
-기로 했어요 "…ishga qaror qildim / kelishdik" degan maʼnoni bildiradi.

column1: Take "-다" off the verb and add "-기로 했어요". The final consonant does not matter.
column2: Feʼldan "-다" ni olib, "-기로 했어요" qoʻshing. Oxirgi undosh ahamiyatga ega emas.

column1: Because it has already been decided, it is usually used in the past form, like "-기로 했어요".
column2: Allaqachon qaror qilingani uchun u odatda "-기로 했어요" kabi oʻtgan zamon shaklida ishlatiladi.

column1: -(으)려고 해요 is a plan in your mind, and "-기로 했어요" is something already decided or promised with another person.
column2: -(으)려고 해요 — bu xayolingizdagi reja, "-기로 했어요" esa boshqa odam bilan allaqachon kelishilgan yoki vaʼda qilingan narsa.

column1: For deciding not to do something, use "안 -기로 했어요" or "-지 않기로 했어요".
column2: Biror narsani qilmaslikka qaror qilsangiz, "안 -기로 했어요" yoki "-지 않기로 했어요" ishlating.

column1: We agreed to meet on the weekend.
I decided to live in the dormitory for one more year.
column2: Yotoqxonada yana bir yil yashashga qaror qildim.

column1: Let's agree to have the group meeting tomorrow.
What are you doing on Sunday?
Aisha and I are going to play soccer. (We agreed to.)
Of course. We agreed to meet at the sports field at 10.
column2: Albatta. Soat oʻnda sport maydonchasida uchrashishga kelishdik.

column1: A soft way to suggest doing something. It is like "How about …?" or "Why don't you …?" in English.
column2: Biror narsani yumshoq taklif qilish usuli. Oʻzbek tilidagi "…sangiz qanday?" yoki "…sangiz-chi?" ga oʻxshaydi.

column1: -는 게 어때요? is a soft way to suggest something.
column2: -는 게 어때요? biror narsani yumshoq taklif qilish usuli.

column1: Take "-다" off the verb and add "-는 게 어때요?". The final consonant does not matter. A ㄹ final consonant drops (만들다 → 만드는 게).
column2: Feʼldan "-다" ni olib, "-는 게 어때요?" qoʻshing. Oxirgi undosh ahamiyatga ega emas. Oxirgi undosh ㄹ tushib qoladi (만들다 → 만드는 게).

column1: 게 is a short form of "것이". The formal form is "-는 것이 어떻습니까?".
column2: 게 — "것이" ning qisqa shakli. Rasmiy shakli "-는 것이 어떻습니까?".

column1: For a stronger suggestion, say "-는 게 좋겠어요": "병원에 가는 게 좋겠어요." (You'd better go to the hospital.)
column2: Kuchliroq taklif uchun "-는 게 좋겠어요" deng: "병원에 가는 게 좋겠어요." (Kasalxonaga borganingiz maʼqul.)

column1: How about going to see a doctor?
My lower back keeps hurting these days.
Then you'd better tell your part-time job boss and take a day off.
column2: Unda qoʻshimcha ishingizdagi xoʻjayinga aytib, bir kun dam olganingiz maʼqul.

column1: Used to tell or advise someone politely. It is like "Please …" in English.
column2: Kimgadir biror narsani muloyimlik bilan aytish yoki maslahat berish uchun ishlatiladi. Oʻzbek tilidagi "…ing / …ng" (marhamat qilib) ga oʻxshaydi.

column1: -(으)세요 is a polite way to tell or advise someone to do something.
column2: -(으)세요 — kimgadir biror narsa qilishni muloyimlik bilan aytish yoki maslahat berish usuli.

column1: With a final consonant add "-으세요"; without one add "-세요". A ㄹ final consonant drops (만들다 → 만드세요).
column2: Oxirgi undosh boʻlsa "-으세요", boʻlmasa "-세요" qoʻshiladi. Oxirgi undosh ㄹ tushib qoladi (만들다 → 만드세요).

column1: In English, "please" comes before the verb, but in Korean the end of the verb changes: "Please sit down" = "앉으세요".
column2: Oʻzbek tilidagi kabi, koreys tilida ham buyruq feʼl oxiridagi qoʻshimcha bilan ifodalanadi: "Oʻtiring" = "앉으세요".

column1: Use it to suggest something good for the listener. When you ask someone to do something for you, "-아/어 주세요" is more polite.
column2: Tinglovchi uchun foydali narsani taklif qilganda ishlating. Kimdandir oʻzingiz uchun biror narsa qilishni soʻraganda "-아/어 주세요" muloyimroq.

column1: 먹다, 마시다 become "드세요", 자다 becomes "주무세요", and 있다 becomes "계세요".
column2: 먹다, 마시다 "드세요" ga, 자다 "주무세요" ga, 있다 esa "계세요" ga aylanadi.

column1: Please write your name here. And please wait a moment.
column2: Ismingizni shu yerga yozing. Va bir oz kutib turing.

column1: Used when you ask someone to do something for you. It is like "Please … (for me)" in English.
column2: Kimdandir oʻzingiz uchun biror narsa qilishni soʻraganda ishlatiladi. Oʻzbek tilidagi "…ib bering" ga oʻxshaydi.

column1: -아/어 주세요 is a request to do something for you.
column2: -아/어 주세요 — siz uchun biror narsa qilishni soʻrash.

column1: Take "요" off the "-아요/어요" form and add "주세요". For nouns, use "noun + 주세요".
column2: -아요/어요 shaklidan "요" ni olib, "주세요" qoʻshing. Otlar uchun "ot + 주세요" ishlating.

column1: 주다 means "to give". After a verb, it means doing something for someone: "도와 주다" = to help (someone).
column2: 주다 "bermoq" degani. Feʼldan keyin u kimdir uchun biror narsa qilishni bildiradi: "도와 주다" = (kimgadir) yordam bermoq. Oʻzbekchadagi "…ib bermoq" kabi.

column1: More polite forms are "-아/어 주시겠어요?" and "-아/어 주실 수 있어요?".
column2: Muloyimroq shakllari: "-아/어 주시겠어요?" va "-아/어 주실 수 있어요?".

column1: Learn these three phrases for when you don't understand: "다시 말해 주세요", "천천히 말해 주세요", "써 주세요".
column2: Tushunmaganingizda ishlatiladigan uchta iborani yodlang: "다시 말해 주세요", "천천히 말해 주세요", "써 주세요".

column1: Professor, I'm sorry, but please say that again.
column2: Professor, kechirasiz, buni yana bir marta aytib bera olasizmi.

column1: Write this word in your notebook three times.
column2: Bu soʻzni daftaringizga uch marta yozing.

column1: Yes, I understand. Please show me once.
column2: Ha, tushundim. Bir marta koʻrsatib bering.

column1: You can write it like this.
This is the most formal way to tell someone to do something. It is used in notices, safety signs, announcements and when speaking to customers.
column2: Bu kimgadir biror narsa qilishni aytishning eng rasmiy usuli. Eʼlonlarda, xavfsizlik belgilarida, xabarnomalarda va mijozlarga gapirganda ishlatiladi.

column1: -(으)십시오 is the most formal way to tell someone to do something, used on signs and in announcements.
column2: -(으)십시오 — kimgadir biror narsa qilishni aytishning eng rasmiy usuli, belgilar va eʼlonlarda ishlatiladi.

column1: With a final consonant add "-으십시오"; without one add "-십시오".
-십시오 is pronounced [십씨오] (sipsio). In writing it ends in "-시오". Writing "-십시요" is wrong.
column2: -십시오 [십씨오] (sipsio) deb talaffuz qilinadi. Yozuvda "-시오" bilan tugaydi. "-십시요" deb yozish xato.

column1: To tell someone not to do something, use "-지 마십시오": "들어가지 마십시오." (Please do not enter.)
column2: Kimgadir biror narsani qilmaslikni aytish uchun "-지 마십시오" ishlating: "들어가지 마십시오." (Iltimos, kirmang.)
